strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: retaining information beyond the context window of offline transformer policies. Combining segment recurrence with return-conditioned action prediction is a practical approach.
T-Maze provides concrete evidence of memory use. RATE-7 achieves 99.3% success at five segments versus 48.9% for DT-7, and replacing memory tokens with noise reduces performance toward chance.

Evaluation covers two memory-dependent environments, four Atari games, and nine MuJoCo dataset settings. Reported results show substantial improvements over DT on Qbert and broadly competitive locomotion performance.
The curriculum, memory perturbation, segment-count, and memory-size ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence. The manuscript also supplies hyperparameters and a code repository link.
weaknesses: Novelty and comparative significance are insufficiently established. The method largely combines existing RMT and Transformer-XL mechanisms with Decision Transformer and curriculum learning. On the central memory-dependent tasks, comparisons are limited to DT and random policies; recurrent policy baselines and a Transformer-XL-only control are missing. These experiments do not establish an advantage over existing memory-capable approaches.

Important comparisons confound memory with other changes. In VizDoom, RATE trains on episode prefixes containing the cue, whereas DT samples random subsequences (Section 4.2). MuJoCo introduces segment-wise return resets without a corresponding DT control. Moreover, RATE without memory tokens already scores 12,300 on Qbert versus 13,518 for RATE and 2,215.8 for DT, showing that most of this improvement does not establish the benefit of the proposed tokens.

The central training algorithm is described inconsistently. Section 3 states that the recurrent memory is detached, then says gradients from the next segment flow through that memory into the preceding segment. These statements require clarification. The gradient truncation schedule, treatment of cached states, and optimizer update procedure need an unambiguous specification to assess learning across segments and reproduce the method.

The VizDoom memory interpretation has an unresolved information-channel confound. Section 4.1 excludes reward observations because they reveal the correct color, but successive reward-updated return-to-go inputs can reveal those rewards. Table 6 explores fixed return conditioning for RATE, but lacks matched DT controls. This prevents clean attribution of the advantage to retaining the initial visual cue.

The claimed statistical significance in VizDoom is not established by the reported evidence: RATE obtains 16.46 ± 6.90 versus 6.08 ± 1.62 for DT90, with these uncertainties labeled standard errors. With only three training seeds and no supporting statistical analysis, this is suggestive rather than convincing evidence of a reliable improvement.

Long-horizon robustness and practical efficiency remain limited. RATE-3 reaches approximately chance performance at nine segments, while RATE-7 falls to 66.1% at twelve. The reported 100-segment success uses memory frozen after the first segment, rather than demonstrating robust recurrent updating. Despite efficiency motivating the approach, no quantitative GPU-memory, throughput, or wall-time comparison establishes its practical scaling advantage.
